note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  • Reduced hearing in the left ear for the past 6 weeks.  
  • Associated intermittent ringing (tinnitus) in the same ear; patient notes that watching TV or listening to music often “solves” (reduces) the ringing. No specific precipitating exposure identified.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  • Current episode: 6 weeks, on-and-off.  
  • Prior episode of similar hearing difficulty about 1 year ago, lasted only a few days and resolved spontaneously.
- ENT symptoms:
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation: none.  
  • Voice change/hoarseness: none.  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling: none.  
  • Nasal/ocular symptoms: none reported.  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea: none.  
  • Swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face): none.  
  • Otologic: unilateral (left) hearing loss, intermittent tinnitus, no ear pain, no discharge, no itching.  
  • Vestibular: occasional mild dizziness/off-balance sensation; no true vertigo, no nausea, no chest pain, no palpitations.  
  • Neck pain/swelling and ear-related headache: none reported.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  • Brief episode of hearing difficulty 1 year ago; no medical evaluation or treatment documented.
  • No prior ear examinations, hospital visits, or medication/injection therapy for this problem.
- Allergies: not mentioned (not documented).
- Current medications: none reported.
- Social context: Patient at home in a private setting during video consult; no one else mentioned as present.

Objective:
- Observable swelling/distribution: not visualized via video; none reported.
- Airway/breathing: no distress reported.
- Mental status: alert, oriented; reports mild intermittent dizziness only.
- Vitals and physical examination findings: Not recorded.
- Presence of companion: not present/not mentioned.

Assessment:
- Unilateral left-sided hearing loss with intermittent tinnitus and mild imbalance.  
- Most likely preliminary considerations: impacted cerumen or other external/middle-ear obstruction; alternative inner-ear pathology less likely but to be considered.  
- No red-flag ENT airway symptoms.  
- Name discrepancy noted: patient states “Jack Smith,” clinician addressed him as “John” at one point (conflict noted).

Plan:
- Arrange face-to-face clinic visit within 4–5 days for otoscopic examination to assess for ear-canal obstruction and evaluate tympanic membrane.  
  • Doctor will message admin team to schedule appointment; patient instructed to call support team once the note is filed to finalize slot.  
- Provide patient education: link to tinnitus information leaflet pasted into visit notes for reading prior to appointment.  
- Safety-netting / escalation:  
  • If any new or worsening symptoms arise before the clinic visit (e.g., increasing hearing loss, severe dizziness, pain, discharge), patient to book another video appointment.  
- Follow-up: in-person GP/ENT assessment as above; further management dependent on otoscopy findings.

Quality checks:
● Missing but expected elements: formal allergy list; current medication list; past medical/surgical history; otoscopic and tuning-fork examination; vital signs; documentation of noise exposure history; clarification whether tinnitus is alleviated vs triggered by sound.  
● Internal conflicts: patient identified himself as “Jack,” clinician used “John” once—name discrepancy (conflict noted).  
● Transcript quality: clear overall; occasional short inaudible pauses but adequate for clinical documentation.
